questions.question: What does 1 + 2 * 3 + 4 evaluate to, and why?
options: 21, because Haskell evaluates strictly left to right
11, because * has higher precedence than +, so 2 * 3 reduces first
9, because + is evaluated before *
A type error, because the expression mixes + and *
questions.explanation: Multiplication binds tighter than addition, so 2 * 3 becomes 6 first, giving 1 + 6 + 4 = 11 — exactly the reduction shown for 1 + 2 * 3 just above.
optionFeedback: Haskell does not evaluate strictly left to right when operators of different precedence are mixed; * is applied before the surrounding + operations regardless of position.
Correct. 2 * 3 reduces to 6 first because * has higher precedence, leaving 1 + 6 + 4, which is 11.
This has the precedence backwards — * binds tighter than +, not the other way around.
Mixing + and * is completely ordinary arithmetic in Haskell; there is no type conflict between two numeric operators.

questions.question: Why does 9 + -7 produce an error while 9 + (-7) does not?
options: Haskell reads the - after + as subtraction, so 9 + -7 parses as an incomplete '9 + minus 7' rather than '9 plus negative 7'
GHCi has a bug that misreads negative numbers
9 + -7 is fine; the error only happens with larger numbers
Negative numbers are not allowed anywhere in Haskell
questions.explanation: Haskell writes negative numbers with a leading -, but that same symbol also means subtraction. Straight after an operator, GHCi cannot tell which meaning you intend, so the brackets in (-7) remove the ambiguity by making it unmistakably one literal value.
optionFeedback: Correct. This is exactly the rule stated just above: brackets are required around a negative number that immediately follows an operator.
This is standard, documented Haskell parsing behaviour, not a bug.
The size of the numbers is irrelevant; 9 + -1 fails for the identical reason.
Negative numbers are used throughout this course — cube (-2) appears later in this very lesson — they just need brackets in certain positions.

check-let-and-it-at-the-prompt.title: Check: let and it at the prompt

questions.question: You quit GHCi after typing let radius = 5, then start a fresh GHCi session and immediately type radius * 2. What happens?
options: It evaluates to 10, because let bindings are saved automatically between sessions
An error, because radius is not in scope — prompt definitions are lost when GHCi closes, and nothing has (re)defined radius in the new session
It evaluates to 0, because unset names default to zero
GHCi asks you to re-enter the value of radius before continuing
questions.explanation: The callout states this exactly: expressions and definitions entered at the prompt are lost when GHCi closes. A brand-new session starts with nothing you typed in the old one, so radius is simply undefined until you bind it again.
optionFeedback: There is no autosave for prompt bindings; that is precisely why the lesson recommends saving real work in a .hs file instead.
Correct — this is the exact scenario the callout warns about: nothing entered at the prompt survives GHCi closing.
Haskell has no such default; an unbound name is not silently treated as any value, including zero — it is simply not in scope.
GHCi does not prompt for missing bindings; it reports 'Variable not in scope' and stops there.

questions.question: Why does Haskell reject an if expression with no else branch, while Java accepts an if statement with no else?
options: Haskell simply has stricter syntax rules for no particular reason
In Haskell, if...then...else is an expression that must produce a value on every path; a missing else would leave no value for the False case, so the expression could not have a type
Java's if is also an expression, so the two languages behave identically
Haskell requires else only when the condition might be True
questions.explanation: Every Haskell expression must have a type, and its type comes from the value it produces. An if with no else would have nothing to produce when the condition is False, so GHC cannot assign it a type at all — it is rejected before evaluation even starts.
optionFeedback: There is a precise structural reason, not an arbitrary style rule: if...then...else must produce a value on both branches because it is an expression.
Correct. This is the exact reasoning given in the lesson: without an else, the expression would have no value when the condition is False, so it could not have a type.
Java's if is a statement that performs an action; it does not need to produce a value, which is why an else-less if is legal there but not in Haskell.
The rule applies regardless of which branch is actually taken at run time — GHC checks types before any evaluation happens, so it cannot know in advance which branch will run.

questions.question: cube x = x * x * x is defined at the prompt. What does :type cube report, and why does it mention Num a rather than a concrete type like Integer?
options: cube :: Integer -> Integer, because all numbers default to Integer
cube :: Num a => a -> a, because cube was never given an explicit signature, so GHC infers the most general type that makes x * x * x valid
cube :: a -> a, because cube works on any type whatsoever
GHCi cannot report a type for a function defined without a signature
questions.explanation: Without an explicit signature, GHC infers the most general type consistent with the definition. x * x * x only requires that x support multiplication, i.e. belong to the Num class — it does not require any one specific numeric type, so GHC leaves it general.
optionFeedback: This is what defaulting does when you evaluate an ambiguous numeric expression directly, but :type on a function definition reports the general inferred type, not a defaulted one.
Correct — this is exactly what the transcript in this section shows: cube :: Num a => a -> a.
cube is not fully unconstrained: x must support multiplication, which not every type does (a Bool, for instance, cannot be multiplied), so a itself is restricted to Num a.
:type works perfectly well on functions with inferred types; GHC always has some type to report once a definition type-checks.

questions.question: You want to know which module defines the not function. Which command answers that directly?
options: :type not
:info not
:load not
:browse not
questions.explanation: :info shows a -- Defined in ‘...’ comment naming the module. :type only reports not's type signature, Bool -> Bool, with no information about where it comes from.
optionFeedback: :type not reports not :: Bool -> Bool — useful, but it says nothing about which module defined the name.
Correct. :info's whole purpose is to answer 'what is this name and where did it come from', including the defining module.
:load expects a filename ending in .hs, not the name of an existing function; this would fail.
:browse expects a module name (like :browse Prelude), not a single function name.

deeper-reasoning-working-at-the-prompt.title: Deeper reasoning: working at the prompt

questions.question: A student spends an evening defining cube and isVowel at the GHCi prompt, then closes the window. The next day they reopen GHCi, type cube 3, and see that cube is not in scope. They tell a friend that GHC is unreliable. Which response explains the behaviour and gives the better workflow?
options: GHC is unreliable on Windows, and the only fix is to use another operating system.

Definitions typed at the prompt live only in that session and vanish when GHCi closes. That is by design, and it is the reason to keep working definitions in a .hs file. The usual workflow is to experiment at the prompt and then save what worked into a script that can be loaded with :load and refreshed with :reload.
The definitions were saved in a hidden file and will return if the student types :restore.
cube was lost because it was defined without a type signature, and functions that have signatures are saved automatically.
questions.explanation: GHCi is a laboratory and a .hs file is the notebook. The prompt is excellent for quick experiments, but nothing typed there survives the session unless it is copied into a file.
optionFeedback: Nothing is wrong with GHC. Any language's interactive session loses its definitions when it is closed.
Correct. Session state is temporary; a script is how definitions are kept and shared.
There is no such command. GHCi does not save prompt definitions anywhere.
Signatures do not affect persistence. Even a definition with a signature is lost when the session ends unless it is in a file.

questions.question: A student follows lecture slides that show the prompt as Prelude> and sees only ghci> on their own machine. They suspect that their installation is incomplete and that the Prelude is missing. Which explanation is the most accurate?
options: The Prelude is missing. Without it, even 2 + 3 would fail, so the installation must be repaired.

The two prompts are cosmetic differences between GHC versions. The older prompt listed the modules loaded into the session, and Prelude, the standard library module imported automatically, was always among them. Arithmetic, comparisons and putStrLn working at the new prompt show that the Prelude is available, and :set prompt "Prelude> " restores the old style if wanted.
ghci> is the prompt for beginners and Prelude> is the prompt for advanced users, so the student's installation is in beginner mode.
The prompt changed because the student's computer is not connected to the internet.
questions.explanation: The prompt is only a label. The evidence that the Prelude is present is behaviour: if 2 + 3 and not True evaluate, the standard definitions are in scope. The prompt text can be changed with :set prompt.
optionFeedback: If the Prelude were missing, nothing in the first lessons would work. The working prompt arithmetic is itself the proof that it is present.
Correct. The change is cosmetic, and the same prompt command can reproduce either form.
There are no beginner and advanced prompt modes. Newer releases simply print a shorter prompt.
GHCi does not depend on an internet connection to choose its prompt.

questions.question: A student defines a function at the prompt, finds that cube -2 produces a confusing error about a function that cannot be shown, and "fixes" it by typing cube 0-2. No error appears, and the answer is accepted. Which evaluation of this fix is correct?
options: The fix is correct. Haskell reads 0-2 as the number negative two, so cube 0-2 computes the cube of -2.

The fix is wrong but silent. cube -2 fails because - is read as subtraction, so GHC sees cube minus 2 and cannot make sense of subtracting a number from a function. cube 0-2 is read as (cube 0) - 2, which is 0 - 2 = -2, not (-2) cubed. Writing cube (-2) gives -8, because the brackets make -2 a single value.
The fix is wrong because negative numbers cannot be used with cube; the function can only accept positive numbers.
The first error appears because cube was defined at the prompt; defining it in a file would allow cube -2 to work.
questions.explanation: Function application binds tighter than any operator, so cube 0-2 means (cube 0) - 2. Because that is well-typed, GHC raises no error and the student gets the wrong value without any warning. Brackets around a negative number make it one literal that becomes the whole argument.
optionFeedback: 0-2 is not a negative literal; it is a subtraction, and application binds tighter than subtraction, so only 0 goes to cube.
Correct. The dangerous part is that the wrong answer is well typed, so only careful reading or a known expected value reveals it.
cube accepts any number, including negative ones. The brackets are only needed to group the sign with the digits.
Where the function is defined makes no difference. The parsing rule that causes the error is part of the language, not of the prompt.
